citeAs: Talmor, A., Herzig, J., Lourie, N., and Berant, J. (2019). CommonsenseQA: A Question Answering Challenge Targeting Commonsense Knowledge. NAACL 2019.
creator: Alon Talmor, Jonathan Herzig, Nicholas Lourie, Jonathan Berant (Tel-Aviv University, Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence)
description: CommonsenseQA is a challenging multiple-choice question answering dataset targeting commonsense knowledge. It contains 12,247 questions generated by crowd workers based on subgraphs from ConceptNet, where each question requires prior commonsense knowledge to answer correctly. Each question has five candidate answers (one correct, four distractors), and the best baseline (BERT-large) achieves only 56% accuracy compared to 89% human performance.
name: CommonsenseQA
publisher: Tel-Aviv University / Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence
rai:annotationsPerItem: Each question was verified by 2 workers during the quality verification phase.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Questions were filtered based on verification: only questions verified by at least one worker who answered correctly were retained. This process filtered out 15% of the questions. Human accuracy on a sample of 100 questions (answered by 5 workers each, majority vote) was 88.9%.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: AMT workers were shown a question concept and three answer concepts from ConceptNet. They were asked to formulate three questions (one per answer concept) such that each question has exactly one of the three target concepts as the correct answer. Workers were instructed to avoid using words strongly related to the answer concept (e.g., not using 'open' when the answer is 'door'). Workers also added two distractors per question: one chosen from ConceptNet concepts with the same relation to the question concept, and one authored manually. A separate disjoint group of workers verified question quality by annotating each question as unanswerable or choosing the correct answer; only questions verified by at least one worker who answered correctly were retained. Only annotators for which at least 75% of their questions passed verification were accepted.
rai:dataBiases: The paper notes that questions are generated freely by workers and often require background knowledge that is trivial to humans but seldom explicitly reported on the web due to reporting bias. The paper also notes that 10 workers formulated more than 85% of the questions despite 122 total formulators contributing, indicating a skewed distribution of question authorship. The paper also discusses that annotation artifacts in similar datasets (e.g., Story Cloze Test) allow models to exploit distributional biases; the dataset design (using semantically similar distractors) was intended to mitigate simple surface-clue exploitation.
rai:dataCollection: Questions were generated by Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) crowd workers. Workers were shown a source concept and three target concepts sampled from ConceptNet subgraphs, and asked to author three multiple-choice questions (one per target concept). Workers also added two additional distractors per question (one selected from ConceptNet, one authored manually). A separate group of workers verified question quality. Web snippets from Google Search were also collected for each question-answer pair to provide textual context.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: ConceptNet knowledge base (version 5.5), containing 32 million triplets of the form (concept1, relation, concept2). A filtered subset of 236,208 triplets was used, organized into approximately 43,000 question sets. Web snippets retrieved via Google Search (first 100 result snippets per question-answer pair, yielding 500 snippets per question) were also collected.
rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Web Scraping, Secondary Data analysis
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is grounded in ConceptNet, which may limit the diversity of commonsense phenomena covered. The best model (BERT-large) achieves only 55.9% accuracy, but learning curve analysis suggests performance would reach approximately 75% with 100k examples, still below human performance. The random split is harder for models that memorize question-concept to answer mappings. Web snippets retrieved via Google Search do not appear to carry sufficient useful information for reading comprehension models.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: ConceptNet triplets were filtered using the following rules: (1) triplets with general relations (e.g., RelatedTo) or relations already well-explored in NLP (e.g., IsA) were removed, retaining 22 relations; (2) triplets where one concept is more than four words or not in English were removed; (3) triplets where the edit distance between the two concepts is too low were removed. This resulted in 236,208 triplets. Questions were then organized into question sets of three triplets sharing the same question concept and relation. The dataset was split 80/10/10 into train/development/test sets using either a random split or a question-concept split (disjoint question concepts across sets).
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to facilitate future work in incorporating commonsense knowledge into NLU systems, advancing the field of machine common sense and natural language understanding.
rai:dataUseCases: Evaluating and developing NLU models on commonsense question answering; benchmarking the ability of models to incorporate commonsense knowledge; studying what commonsense knowledge is captured by current NLU systems and identifying gaps.
